name: Composition over Inheritance
intent: Build behaviour by assembling small parts that an object holds and delegates to, instead of by stretching a class hierarchy, so that variations can be combined freely and a change in one place does not shake every subclass.
scenario: A strategy game has units that can walk, swim or fly, and attack in melee or at range. The first version makes a class for each kind of unit and shares code through a hierarchy. Then designers want a duck that walks, swims and flies, a frog that walks and swims, and a new ability every month.
problem: Inheritance ties a subclass to the internals of its parent: a change that looks safe inside the base class can break subclasses that were never touched. It also fixes one axis of variation in a tree. When a thing varies in two independent ways, the tree needs a class for every combination, and single inheritance cannot reuse more than one parent, so behaviour is copied. A hierarchy that began as a taxonomy turns into an explosion of classes, and it is also one of the common causes of Liskov violations, where a subclass cannot honour what the parent promised.

howItWorks.title: See the coupling in inheritance
howItWorks.text: A subclass depends on what its parent does, not only on what it declares. If the parent's addAll happens to call add, a subclass that counts calls to both counts each unit twice. Change the parent so addAll no longer calls add and the subclass, untouched, is suddenly right, or wrong the other way. This is the fragile base class problem: the parent cannot be changed without knowing every subclass.

howItWorks.title: Notice the taxonomy problem
howItWorks.text: A hierarchy models one question: what kind of thing is this? Units that walk, swim and fly, and attack in melee or at range, answer two independent questions. With every combination in the game, 3 movement abilities and 2 attack styles need 14 classes, 6 abilities need 126, and the code for each ability is copied into every class that cannot inherit it. Adding one more movement ability roughly doubles the classes.

howItWorks.title: Pull each variation out as a part
howItWorks.text: Define a small interface for each axis (how the unit moves, how it attacks) and one class per behaviour. A Unit holds a list of movement parts and one attack part, and delegates to them. A duck is a Unit built with walk, swim and fly and ranged. A new ability is one new class, and every existing combination can use it without being edited.

howItWorks.title: Keep inheritance for real is-a relationships
howItWorks.text: Inheritance still fits when a subclass truly is the parent in every way the parent promises, the contract is small and stable, and the base class was designed to be extended, for example a framework's extension point. Many designs use a shallow hierarchy of one or two levels, with composition for everything that varies.

howItWorks.title: Count the costs of composition too
howItWorks.text: Parts must be assembled somewhere: each unit type is a line of configuration. Delegation means forwarding methods, which is boilerplate in languages without help for it. And composition without clear roles, with parts that all know about each other or a god object that passes everything around, is as hard to follow as a tangled tree. Name each part by the single job it does.

pros: Behaviours combine freely, so new combinations cost no new class
A change inside one part does not reach the others as long as they only meet through a small interface
Parts can be swapped at run time and tested alone
Avoids copying behaviour into classes that cannot inherit it
cons: More small objects and an assembly step to learn and maintain
Delegation boilerplate: wrapping and forwarding calls by hand
The relationships are in wiring code rather than in a type tree, so a reader must follow the assembly to see what a unit does
For a small, stable set of variants, the hierarchy is shorter and easier to read
whenToUse: Something varies on two or more independent axes, such as movement and attack
New variants are expected often and must combine with the existing ones
A base class has become fragile: nobody dares change it
whenNotToUse: A genuine is-a relationship with a small, stable contract, where the subclass can stand in for the parent everywhere
A framework extension point that the framework designed for subclassing
A handful of fixed variants that will not grow, where parts and wiring add more than they remove
pitfalls: Reading the slogan as never use inheritance: it is right for real is-a relationships and for framework hooks, and a ban produces needless wiring
Delegation boilerplate: wrapping an object and forwarding twenty methods by hand, which can hide behaviour that one subclass line would have kept in plain sight
Composition without clear roles: parts with vague names that reach into each other, or a Unit that knows every part, so the tangle has only moved
Using inheritance just to reuse code from a class the subclass is not really a kind of, which is how Liskov violations start
Overriding a method that the parent also calls from other methods, so the subclass depends on how the parent is written, not on what it promises
Deep hierarchies where each level adds one flag or one override and nobody can say what a leaf class does

roles.label: Base class
roles.description: The parent that subclasses inherit from.

roles.label: Subclass
roles.description: A class that extends the parent and relies on how it works.

roles.label: Unit
roles.description: The object that holds parts and delegates to them.

roles.label: Behaviour part
roles.description: A small class for one ability, behind an interface.

quiz.question: A subclass overrides add and addAll to count the units added. Later the base class author rewrites addAll so that it no longer calls add, and changes nothing else. What happens to the subclass?
options: Its counts change, although its own code did not, because it relied on how the base was written.
Nothing changes, because the base class still has the same public methods and signatures.
It no longer compiles, because the override of addAll is now missing a required call to add.
Its counts stay right, because overriding a method makes the subclass independent of the parent.
quiz.explanation: This is the fragile base class problem: the subclass depended on an internal detail, that addAll calls add. Matching signatures do not protect against it. A wrapper that holds the army and counts what it forwards does not depend on that detail.

quiz.question: Units may combine any of 4 movement abilities with one of 2 attack styles, and every combination is needed. Roughly how does a pure inheritance tree compare with composition as abilities are added?
options: Both grow by one class per ability, since each new ability is one new class either way.
Inheritance needs a class per combination, which doubles with each ability, while composition adds one class.
Composition needs a class per combination, because each unit type must be written out as a class.
Inheritance stays smaller, because a shared base class removes the need for separate classes.
quiz.explanation: With every combination needed, a tree needs a class per non-empty set of movements and attack style: 30 for 4 abilities and 2 styles, and one more ability doubles it. Composition adds one behaviour class, and the combination is built at assembly time.

quiz.question: Which situation is a good fit for inheritance, even to someone who prefers composition?
options: A Penguin extending Bird, so that it can reuse the shared code, while overriding fly to throw an error.
A Stack extending List, so that it can reuse the storage while hiding most of the list's methods.
A subclass written to a framework's documented extension point, which is designed to be extended.
A class extending another only to reuse one helper method, with no other relation between them.
quiz.explanation: Inheritance fits a true is-a relationship with a stable, documented contract, such as a framework hook. The other cases reuse code without honouring the parent's contract: they are the usual start of Liskov violations.
